title: Happening right now: -yap
goal: Tell "I read" from "I'm reading", use the *-yap* form on the phone and in quick conversation, and recognize its written form *-moqda*.
bekal: form *oʻqiyapman, oʻqiyapsan, oʻqiyapti…* from any verb stem
choose correctly between the habitual and the progressive form

dialogs.title: Dialog — Alo, hozir nima qilyapsiz?
dialogs.intro: The phone rings. Nilufar is calling Budi, who is out in the street.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: Hello, Budi? Can you hear me?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Yes, I can hear you. Hi, Nilufar!

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: What are you doing right now?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'm heading to the bus stop. I'm waiting for the bus.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: No, it isn't raining. But the wind is strong.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Men choyxonada oʻtiribman. Ustozim ham keldi.
lines.id: I'm sitting in the teahouse. My teacher has come too.
lines.literal: I teahouse-in sitting-I. teacher-my also came.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Yaxshi. Yigirma daqiqadan keyin yetib boraman.
lines.id: OK. I'll be there in twenty minutes.
lines.literal: good. twenty minute-from after reach go-I.

notes: **-yap is the spoken form; -moqda is the written form.** They mean the same. *Ketyapman* and *ketmoqdaman* both mean "I'm leaving", but you hear the first in the street and read the second in the newspaper. This course uses *-yap* because that's what you'll use.
**The third person ends in -yapti, not -yapdi.** *U ketyapti* (he's leaving), *Yomgʻir yogʻyapti* (it's raining). This is the only form you need to learn separately.

**Oʻtiribman = "I'm sitting".** A few verbs of position — sit, stand, lie, wear — use the *-ib* form + person ending instead of *-yap*: *oʻtiribman*, *turibman*, *yotibman*. *Oʻtiryapman* is also used, but it stresses the act of sitting down, not the state of already sitting.

**Yetib bormoq = "to arrive".** A compound verb: *yetmoq* (to reach) + *bormoq* (to go). Uzbek chains two verbs to add a sense of direction or completion — a tool you'll start to recognize on your own over time, a bit like English phrasal verbs.

grammars.title: Stem + -yap + person
body: The formula is that short. Take the stem, attach *-yap*, then the person ending you've known since unit 1.
after: Unlike the habitual form, **there's no choice between -a and -y** here: *-yap* attaches straight to the stem, whatever its last letter. *bor-yapman*, *ishla-yapman*, *ich-yapman*.
**The negative inserts -ma- before -yap**: *bormayapman* (I'm not going), *yogʻmayapti* (it isn't raining). The order stays fixed: stem → *-ma-* → *-yap* → person.
Questions work as usual, with *-mi* at the end: *Eshityapsizmi?* (Can you hear me?), *Nima qilyapti?* (What is he doing?).

grammars.title: Habitual or progressive? One question decides
body: English already separates "I read" from "I'm reading", so this distinction will feel familiar. Ask yourself: **is this happening right now?**
after: Look at the last row: **future plans use the habitual form**, not the progressive. *Ertaga boraman* = "I'm going tomorrow". Unlike English "I'm going", the *-yap* form is only for things actually in progress as you speak.
Time words that usually go with *-yap*: *hozir* (now), *ayni paytda* (at the moment), *hozirda*. Those that go with the habitual: *har kuni*, *odatda* (usually), *har doim*.
When in doubt, choose the habitual form. It's broader and rarely sounds wrong; *-yap* used in the wrong place sounds odd straight away.

sections.title: Making a phone call from start to finish

blocks.text: The phone is the scariest place for beginners because there's no face to read. These ten phrases cover almost all of it.

head: Oʻzbekcha
Say it
English
rows: You're busy, I'll call back later.

blocks.text: *Qoʻngʻiroq* literally means "bell", and *qoʻngʻiroq qilmoq* means "to ring the bell" — the Uzbek way of saying "to call" (compare English "give me a ring"). The short form *telefon qilmoq* is also common.

sections.title: Weather: a topic that's always safe

blocks.text: Uzbekistan has a continental desert climate: summers can hit 45 °C, winters can drop below zero. So weather isn't empty small talk there — it really shapes people's day.

The most common question: *Bugun havo qanday?* (What's the weather like today?) — answered with *Havo issiq*, *Havo sovuq*, *Yomgʻir yogʻyapti*, *Qor yogʻyapti*. Notice that rain and snow use the same verb, *yogʻmoq* (to fall from the sky).
⚠️ *Havo* means **air and weather** at once — from the Arabic *hawāʾ* (air). *Issiq* (hot) and *sovuq* (cold), on the other hand, are native Turkic words: Turkish has *sıcak* and *soğuk*.
